title: Women receive less active medical treatment than men, raising concerns for healthcare AI
key_facts: University of St Andrews researchers reviewed 1,112 published studies, then those that directly compared care given to male and female patients; the research was published in PLOS ONE.

Among 38 studies that analysed patient records, 33 reported a significant difference in the treatment received; women with the same condition appeared less likely to be offered active management such as surgery, a stent or stronger pain relief.
The pattern appeared in cardiology, surgery, transplantation and emergency medicine, and in most studies it remained after statistical adjustment.
The review does not show every difference was discriminatory or clinically inappropriate; almost none of the studies referred to a guideline recommending different treatment by sex.
Of studies in the period examined, 551 looked at inequality affecting doctors and other health professionals while only 41 looked at what happened to patients.
The researchers warn AI trained on records and literature with unexplained disparities could reproduce them, and intend to test whether generative AI produces similar treatment differences.
Digital Journal adds Canadian context (research funding, digital-health policy); this is its own commentary beyond the study.
quote_evidence: Among 38 studies that analysed patient records, 33 reported a significant difference in the treatment received.
The review does not demonstrate that every difference in treatment was discriminatory or clinically inappropriate.
The St Andrews researchers now intend to test whether generative AI systems produce similar treatment differences.
why_it_matters_hint: If medical records carry unexplained gaps in how women are treated, AI trained on them could repeat the gaps; the researchers have not yet tested that.
event_date: Study publication date not stated; Digital Journal article dated 10 Oct 2026
